title: Cyanohydrin formation
subtitle: Cyanide adds to acetone; HCN protonates the alkoxide and regenerates cyanide

reactants.caption: acetone + cyanide + HCN
reactants.learnerPrompt: Cyanide is the nucleophile. Draw its attack on acetone.
hintTiers: Which atom of cyanide carries the negative charge, and which atom of acetone is electron-poor?
The carbon lone pair of cyanide forms a new C–C bond to the carbonyl carbon, and the C=O π pair moves onto oxygen. Two arrows.
Cyanide carbon lone pair → new C–C bond to the carbonyl carbon; C=O π bond → lone pair on oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Cyanide reacts through carbon, which carries the charge, and makes a strong C–C bond.
The carbonyl oxygen is electron-rich. Cyanide attacks the electron-poor carbonyl carbon.
Cyanide and HCN just swap a proton: nothing changes. Cyanide must attack the carbonyl carbon.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: cyanide attacks the carbonyl carbon. That carbon now has five bonds: move the C=O π pair.

alkoxide.caption: alkoxide + HCN
hintTiers: Which species in the flask is an acid?
The alkoxide oxygen takes the proton of HCN. The H–C bonding pair stays on carbon, so a new cyanide ion forms. Two arrows.
Alkoxide oxygen lone pair → new O–H bond to the proton of HCN; H–C bond of HCN → lone pair on its carbon.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Losing cyanide just reverses the addition; cyanohydrin formation is reversible. Protonate the alkoxide instead.
The carbon of HCN is not the target. Its proton is acidic (pKa about 9): the alkoxide is a base.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Good: the alkoxide takes the proton of HCN. Where does the H–C bonding pair go?

steps.explanationAfterStep: Cyanide is small and strongly nucleophilic. Its carbon lone pair forms the new C–C bond and the C=O π electrons move onto oxygen.
HCN (pKa about 9) protonates the alkoxide and gives back cyanide. HCN alone reacts slowly: a little cyanide is needed as the nucleophile.

mechanismSummary: The carbon lone pair of cyanide attacks the carbonyl carbon and the C=O π electrons move onto oxygen. HCN protonates the alkoxide, giving the cyanohydrin and a new cyanide ion, so cyanide is a catalyst.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 6
